title: Book 3 — Thalia, Chapter 398
paragraphs: It was against this Amasis that Cambyses son of Cyrus was making his expedition, taking with him not only the other peoples over whom he ruled but also Greeks, both Ionians and Aiolians; and the cause of the expedition was as follows. Cambyses sent an envoy to Egypt and asked Amasis to give him his daughter, making the request on the advice of an Egyptian who urged it on Amasis out of a grudge, for the following reason: at the time when Cyrus had sent to Amasis asking for a physician of the eyes, the best in Egypt, Amasis had picked him out of all the physicians in Egypt and torn him away from his wife and children, and handed him over to Persia. Having this grievance, the Egyptian urged Cambyses on by advising him to ask Amasis for his daughter, so that Amasis would either be grieved if he gave her, or if he refused to give her, would offend Cambyses. Amasis, vexed and afraid of the power of the Persians, knew neither how to give nor how to refuse, for he was well aware that Cambyses meant to keep her not as a wife but as a concubine. Reckoning it this way, he did the following: there was a daughter of the former king Apries, very tall and of comely form, the only surviving member of his house, and her name was Nitetis. This girl Amasis adorned with fine clothing and gold, and sent off to Persia as his own daughter. But after a time, when Cambyses greeted her, calling her by the name of her father, the girl said to him: “O king, you do not realize how you have been deceived by Amasis; for he dressed me up in finery and sent me off, giving me to you as his own daughter, whereas in truth I am the daughter of Apries, against whom Amasis rose up along with the Egyptians and murdered him, though he was his lord and master.” These words, and the occasion that produced them, led Cambyses son of Cyrus against Egypt, moved to very great anger.
